findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById will not remove credential from federated storage
findings.body: When `getCredential` returns a credential from federated storage (the first branch of `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`), calling `removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())` attempts to remove the credential from local storage only. The ID returned by a federated storage provider's `getCredentials()` method is typically a locally-generated UUID (as seen in the test storage's `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues` call), which does not exist in local storage. This means that when all recovery codes are used and the credential resides in federated storage, the credential is never actually removed. The stale credential persists in the external storage, and subsequent authentication attempts may continue to find it via `getCredential`, leading to a state where `allCodesUsed()` is true but the credential is never cleaned up.

findings.title: NoSuchElementException if no recovery code credential exists
findings.body: The call `credentialModelOpt.get()` on line 19 will throw `NoSuchElementException` if the Optional is empty (i.e., the user has no recovery code credential in either federated or local storage). While the bean is presumably only instantiated when the credential is expected to exist, a race condition or misconfiguration could cause this to surface as an unhandled 500 error to the user. The previous code had the same pattern (`.findFirst().get()`), but the refactoring introduces a slightly different code path that could expose this more readily if `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` and `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream()` both return empty.

findings.title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are passed to external user storage
findings.body: The `createRecoveryCodesCredential` method serializes the raw generated codes to JSON and passes them to the user storage via `UserCredentialModel`. The `credentialModel` parameter (which contains hashed codes) is only used for the local storage fallback. This means any external user storage provider receives the plaintext recovery codes. If the external storage is compromised, all recovery codes are exposed. While this mirrors the existing OTP pattern (raw secret passed to user storage), recovery codes are bearer tokens that grant full access, making their exposure more critical. The Javadoc should explicitly document that user storage providers receive raw codes and are responsible for hashing them, or the API should be designed to pass hashed codes and let the storage provider handle verification differently.

findings.title: getCredential may return a stale federated credential when both federated and local credentials exist
findings.body: The `getCredential` method checks federated credentials first via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`, then falls back to local storage. If a user has recovery codes in both federated and local storage (e.g., after a storage provider is added or during migration), the method will always return the federated credential, potentially ignoring a newer or more up-to-date local credential. There is no mechanism to detect or resolve this conflict, which could lead to authentication failures if the federated credential is outdated.

findings.title: getCredentials creates a new credential model with a different ID than what was stored
findings.body: In `getCredentials`, a new `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` is created via `createFromValues` each time the method is called, which generates a fresh UUID. This ID differs from the one stored in `myUser.recoveryCodes` (set during `updateCredential`). Any operation that relies on the credential ID for lookups or removal (such as `removeStoredCredentialById` in the authenticator) will fail because the ID is ephemeral and not persisted. This accurately models a real-world federated storage but also demonstrates why the `removeStoredCredentialById` approach in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` is broken for federated credentials.
